items.q: How does the IoC/DI container work? Bean scopes and lifecycle?
items.a:
The container [[g:inverts control]]: you declare beans, the container creates/wires/manages their lifecycle.

DI removes manual `new` calls → easier to test (mock), easier to swap out.

**Scope:**
- [[b:singleton]] (default): 1 instance/context
- [[b:prototype]]: a new instance every time it's fetched
- web scope: [[b:request/session]]

**Lifecycle:** instantiate → DI → `@PostConstruct` → use → `@PreDestroy`.

:::warn Trap
injecting prototype into a singleton → [[r:it's only created once]]. You need `ObjectProvider`/`@Lookup` to get a fresh instance each time.
:::

:::deep
The container has two phases:
- [[b:BeanDefinition]]: reads metadata (can be modified via `BeanFactoryPostProcessor`)
- [[b:instantiation]]: DI, `BeanPostProcessor` wraps the AOP proxy

Prefer [[g:constructor injection]] (immutable, easy to test, detects circular dependencies at startup) over field injection (hides dependencies, hard to test, forces reflection).

- a circular dependency between two constructor-injected singletons → [[g:fail-fast]] (good); fix by splitting responsibilities, [[r:don't use `@Lazy` to hide a design smell]]
- request/session scope needs a scoped proxy to be injected into a singleton
:::

items.q: How does @Transactional actually run? Why does self-invocation lose the transaction?
items.a:
Spring uses an [[g:AOP proxy]] (JDK dynamic proxy if there's an interface, CGLIB if it's a class). The proxy opens/commits/rolls back the tx around the method. The logic lives in the outer proxy, [[o:not in the bean's own bytecode]]. [[r:Self-invocation]]: calling `this.method()` within the same bean → goes straight to `this`, bypassing the proxy → the annotation has no effect. - fix: split into a separate bean, self-injection, or AspectJ weaving - similarly: `private`/`final` methods can't be proxied **Code where the transaction is silently lost:** 
@Service
class BookingService {
    
    public void confirmAll(List<Long> ids) {
        for (Long id : ids) {
            confirm(id);      // = this.confirm(id) → doesn't go through the proxy → NO transaction
        }
    }
    
    @Transactional
    public void confirm(Long id) { /* ... */ }
}
    
// Fix: split into another bean, so the call leaves and re-enters through the proxy
@Service
class BookingConfirmer {
    @Transactional
    public void confirm(Long id) { /* ... */ }
}
:::warn Money trap by default only RuntimeException/Error trigger rollback. A checked exception [[r:does NOT auto-rollback]] unless `rollbackFor` is set. ::: :::deep - JDK dynamic proxy (with an interface) vs CGLIB (subclass — can't proxy `final`/`private`/`static`) - advice sits on the outer proxy → every self-invocation bypasses it - correct fixes: split into another bean, `AopContext.currentProxy()` (needs exposeProxy), or AspectJ weaving (also intercepts self-calls) The transaction is bound to a [[b:thread]] via `TransactionSynchronizationManager` (ThreadLocal) → jumping to another thread (`@Async`, reactive, parallelStream) [[r:loses the tx context]]. [[r:Critical fintech trap]]: calling an external API (PSP/GDS) inside a tx → holds the DB connection too long → pool exhaustion + prolonged locking. :::

items.q: Propagation REQUIRED / REQUIRES_NEW / NESTED — when to use each?
items.a:
PropagationBehaviourUse when
REQUIREDjoins the existing tx or creates a new onedefault — shared commit/rollback
REQUIRES_NEWsuspends the outer tx, opens an independent oneaudit log must persist even if the business tx rolls back
NESTEDsavepoint within the current txpartial rollback back to a savepoint
[[o:REQUIRES_NEW occupies 2 connections at once]] → watch the pool. Isolation can also be configured here (fintech usually uses READ COMMITTED/REPEATABLE READ + deliberate row locking). **Three nested methods and the resulting rollback:** 
@Transactional                                // TX-1 opens here
public void pay(Long bookingId) {
    ledger.debit(bookingId);                   // REQUIRED  → runs within TX-1
    audit.log("PAY_ATTEMPT", bookingId);        // REQUIRES_NEW → TX-2, commits separately
    promo.apply(bookingId);                   // NESTED → savepoint within TX-1
    throw new PaymentFailedException();        // TX-1 rolls back
}
// Result: the debit is rolled back, promo is lost too (its savepoint sits inside TX-1),
// but the audit row STILL remains — that's exactly why REQUIRES_NEW exists.
    
@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
public void log(String type, Long id) { /* ... */ }
    
@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.NESTED)
public void apply(Long id) { /* an error here only rolls back to the savepoint */ }
:::deep - `REQUIRES_NEW` suspends the outer tx and opens a [[r:second connection]] → doubles the pressure on HikariCP under load, prone to pool deadlock (the outer tx holds connection A while waiting on connection B when the pool is exhausted) - `NESTED` uses a JDBC savepoint (not every DB/driver supports it well) **OTA deep dive:** - writing *audit/outbox* entries should [[g:share the tx (REQUIRED)]] to stay atomic with the business operation - REQUIRES_NEW only makes sense when the audit event must be saved even if the business operation fails :::

items.q: Spring AOP: how does the proxy work, and what are its limitations?
items.a:
AOP separates [[g:cross-cutting concerns]] (tx, logging, security, retry) from business logic via *advice* wrapped around a *pointcut*. Spring AOP is [[b:proxy-based (runtime)]]: - it only intercepts calls made *through* the proxy to a Spring bean's public methods - it [[r:does not intercept]] self-calls, private methods, or objects created with `new` If you need more power (constructors, fields, self-calls) → use [[b:AspectJ]] (compile-time/load-time weaving). **Why `private` and `final` methods can't be advised:** 
@Service
class PricingService {
    
    @Cacheable("fares")
    public Fare lookup(String route) { /* ... */ }      // works: called from outside through the proxy
    
    @Cacheable("fares")
    private Fare lookupRaw(String route) { /* ... */ }   // silently does nothing
    
    @Cacheable("fares")
    public final Fare lookupFinal(String r) { /* ... */ } // silently does nothing
}
    
// CGLIB generates a subclass at runtime — whatever can't be overridden can't be advised:
// class PricingService$$SpringCGLIB extends PricingService {
//     public Fare lookup(String r) { ...advice...; return super.lookup(r); }  // OK
//     private/final methods can't be reached by the subclass → advice can never be inserted
// }
:::deep - AspectJ inserts bytecode directly → can intercept constructors, field access, self-calls, non-Spring objects, but the build is more complex (weaver/agent) - ordering multiple aspects via `@Order` (important when tx + retry + logging overlap) - performance: the proxy adds one extra call layer (negligible); an overly broad pointcut makes reasoning harder Deep dive: typical cross-cutting concerns besides tx are retry, rate-limit, audit, metrics — [[r:but don't hide business logic inside an aspect]]. :::

items.q: How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work under the hood?
items.a:
Boot scans auto-config classes (declared in `...AutoConfiguration.imports`), applying them conditionally via [[g:@Conditional]]:
- `@ConditionalOnClass` — is the library on the classpath?
- `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` — has the user not already defined one?
- `@ConditionalOnProperty` — enabled by a property?

→ 'HikariCP is on the classpath ⇒ auto-configure a DataSource'; if you declare your own bean, Boot [[g:steps aside]].

:::tip Bottom line
'convention over configuration' = auto-config + starters. Debug with `--debug` to see the conditions report (matched/unmatched).
:::

:::deep
Boot reads the auto-config list from `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` (replacing the old `spring.factories`), orders them with `@AutoConfigureBefore/After/Order`, and applies `@Conditional` in this order: classpath → user bean → property → web type.

- writing a company-wide [[g:custom starter]] = an auto-config module + `OnMissingBean` (so other teams can override) + `@ConfigurationProperties`
- [[r:Trap]]: wrong auto-config ordering causes wrong bean overrides; too many conditionals slow down startup
:::

items.q: What is a starter dependency and why is it convenient?
items.a:
A starter (e.g. `spring-boot-starter-web`) is a POM 'bundle' that gathers compatible dependencies for a single purpose (web = Spring MVC + Tomcat + Jackson...).

One line instead of declaring and aligning versions for dozens of libraries. Versions are aligned by Boot's [[g:parent BOM]].

:::warn Interview trap
The follow-up question is almost always 'how does a starter differ from auto-configuration?'. A starter is just a POM that pulls in dependencies, [[o:it contains no configuration logic]]; the actual auto-configuration lives in `spring-boot-autoconfigure` with `@Conditional` classes (03-spring-boot-deep-build.auto-configuration-build.q1). Proof: pull in a starter and exclude auto-config, it still runs; conversely you can declare the dependency yourself and auto-config still kicks in.
:::

:::deep
- a starter is a 'meta' POM (little/no code) that bundles compatible dependencies + activates the matching auto-config
- transitive versions are aligned by the `spring-boot-dependencies` BOM → declaring a dependency [[g:needs no version]]
- upgrading Boot means upgrading the whole 'basket' of libraries that have been tested together (reduces jar hell)
- writing your own `company-payments-starter` standardizes config/observability across services (platform engineering)

[[r:Trap]]: overriding a transitive version in the BOM must be done carefully (can break tested compatibility); use `dependency:tree` to check.
:::

items.q: Deep-dive POM: dependencyManagement, BOM, scope, transitive dependencies, exclusion — what do you need to know?
items.a:
- [[b:dependencyManagement / BOM]]: centralizes version declarations (import BOM with scope `import`); child modules inherit them
- [[b:scope]]: `compile` (default), `provided` (supplied by the container), `runtime` (JDBC driver), `test`, `import`
- [[b:transitive dependency]]: a dependency of a dependency; conflicts are resolved by [[o:'nearest wins']]
- [[b:exclusion]]: excludes an unwanted transitive dependency
- distinguish *plugin* (build-time) from *dependency* (the app's libraries)

Golden command: `mvn dependency:tree` to inspect and untangle conflicts.

:::tip Bottom line
transitive + nearest-wins + BOM are the key to avoiding 'jar hell' and `NoSuchMethodError` caused by version mismatches.
:::

:::deep
- [[o:nearest-wins]] resolves conflicts (shallowest depth wins, NOT the highest version) → can sometimes pull in an unexpectedly old version, so pin it explicitly in `dependencyManagement` to [[g:'pin']] it
- `<scope>import</scope>` in dependencyManagement imports a BOM (e.g. Spring Cloud)
- `optional=true` stops a transitive dependency from propagating further; `provided` for things supplied by the container (servlet/lombok)
- `dependency:tree -Dverbose` + `dependency:analyze` (used-but-undeclared / declared-but-unused)

Deep dive: runtime `NoSuchMethodError`/`NoClassDefFoundError` is usually caused by mismatched transitive versions → pinning the BOM + exclusions fixes 'jar hell' at the root.
:::

items.q: Maven vs Gradle — what's the difference, and when to pick which?
items.a:
MavenGradle
Syntaxdeclarative XMLDSL (Groovy/Kotlin)
Speedstable, slowerincremental + build cache + daemon → fast
Customizationstrict conventionflexible build logic
Good forsimple projects, easy onboardinglarge / multi-module projects
:::deep - Gradle is fast thanks to [[g:incremental build]] (only rebuilds what changed) + [[g:build cache]] (reuses output, even remote/CI) + configuration cache + daemon → CI time drops from minutes to seconds for small changes - Maven compensates with [[g:determinism]], strict convention, easy to read/onboard, a huge plugin ecosystem, and 'no custom code' means fewer build bugs Deep dive: pick Gradle for monorepos/multi-module projects needing speed & complex build logic (Android/Kotlin); pick Maven for simplicity and stability. Both support reproducible builds & BOMs (supply-chain security). :::

items.q: Spring profiles & externalized config — best practices for managing configuration?
items.a:
Separate config from code ([[g:12-factor]]): `application-{profile}.yml`, env vars, secret managers.

**Priority order (highest → lowest):**
- command-line args
- env vars
- `application-{profile}.yml`
- `application.yml`
- defaults in code

[[r:Never hardcode secrets]] in the repo; use Vault/Secrets Manager + a config server for multiple services.

:::deep
- do NOT commit secrets to the repo/image; inject them at runtime via env/volume from Vault/AWS Secrets Manager/K8s Secret (+KMS)
- profiles for environment (`dev/staging/prod`) and for features (`@Profile`)
- for multiple services → Spring Cloud Config/Consul + dynamic refresh (`@RefreshScope`) to change config without redeploying

- [[r:Trap]]: a profile-specific override silently causes 'works fine locally, breaks in prod'; storing sensitive config in a ConfigMap instead of a Secret
- config is a kind of API too — version it and audit changes (GitOps)
:::

items.q: @Async and @Scheduled — what should you watch out for?
items.a:
- [[b:@Async]] runs a method on a different thread pool (also proxy-based → self-calls have no effect); configure a dedicated executor, [[r:don't rely on the default unbounded pool]]
- [[b:@Scheduled]] for cron/fixed-rate jobs; with multiple instances you must avoid duplicate runs (ShedLock/distributed lock or leader election)

:::deep
[[r:Production trap]]: `@Async` defaults to `SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor` (spawns a new thread every time, NOT bounded) → under high load this explodes thread count/OOMs.
- you must define a dedicated `ThreadPoolTaskExecutor` (core/max/queueCapacity)
- remember `queueCapacity` must fill up before the pool grows threads toward max (a surprising behaviour)

- `@Async` is also proxy-based → self-calls have no effect, and it loses tx/security/MDC context (needs a TaskDecorator to propagate MDC/trace id)
- `@Scheduled` across N instances runs N times → use ShedLock/distributed lock or leader election

Deep dive: Java 21 — a virtual-thread executor (`newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor`) for `@Async` scales I/O-bound work well without pool tuning.
:::

items.q: Spring Boot Actuator & observing an application?
items.a:
Actuator exposes operational endpoints:
- `/health` (liveness/readiness groups)
- `/metrics` (Micrometer → Prometheus)
- `/info`, `/loggers`...

Integrates with Micrometer + OpenTelemetry to export metrics/traces. [[r:Remember to protect sensitive endpoints]] (auth) + only expose what's needed.

:::deep
- Actuator + Micrometer is a [[g:facade]] that exports metrics to Prometheus/Datadog/OTel (swap the backend without changing code)
- the `/actuator/health` liveness vs readiness groups map directly to K8s probes: readiness includes dependencies (DB, broker), liveness only means 'the process is alive' (avoids a restart loop when the DB is slow)
- custom `HealthIndicator` for business dependencies (GDS/PSP); protect `/env`, `/heapdump` with auth

- wire up Micrometer Tracing + OTel → trace_id flows across services; export custom business metrics (`booking_failed_total`) to alert on SLOs
- [[r:Operational trap]]: high tag cardinality (userId, bookingId) 'blows up' the Prometheus time-series → only tag bounded dimensions (status, endpoint). Use *exemplars* to jump from a metric to its trace.
:::

items.q: Validation (Bean Validation) and centralized error handling?
items.a:
Use `@Valid` + annotations (`@NotNull`, `@Size`, custom constraints) to validate at the [[b:boundary]] (controller/DTO).

Catch errors centrally with `@ControllerAdvice` + `@ExceptionHandler` → return a standard error structure (RFC 7807 problem+json).

Separate [[g:syntactic validation]] (at the boundary) from [[g:business rules]] (in the domain).

:::deep
- [[b:syntactic/format]] at the boundary: DTO + `@Valid` + JSR-380 (`@NotNull`, `@Email`, `@Positive`), validation groups for create vs update
- [[b:business rules]] in the domain: e.g. 'seat count ≤ passenger count' belongs to the aggregate, not an annotation
- custom constraints for reusable rules (valid airport code)
- centralized error handling with `@RestControllerAdvice` → problem+json with field errors

- [[r:Trap]]: validating on the client and then trusting it — you must re-validate on the server (never trust input)
- cross-field validation (return date > departure date) uses a class-level constraint; don't cram complex business rules into an annotation
:::

items.q: How do you configure HikariCP in Spring Boot for a high-traffic service?
items.a:
Tune:
- `maximum-pool-size` (smaller is usually better, matched against the DB's `max_connections` divided by instance count)
- `connection-timeout`
- `max-lifetime` (shorter than the DB/proxy-side timeout)
- `leak-detection-threshold`

[[r:Never call external I/O while holding a connection inside a transaction.]] Monitor the pool via Actuator to catch exhaustion early.

:::deep
- a smaller pool is usually better (Hikari's rule of thumb: connections ≈ (core×2)+effective_spindle; in practice 10–20/instance)
- [[r:the sum of `maximum-pool-size` across all instances must NOT exceed the DB's `max_connections`]] — a common trap when scaling out many pods
- `max-lifetime` should be shorter than the DB/proxy-side timeout (RDS/ProxySQL) to avoid 'dead' connections
- `leak-detection-threshold` catches connections held too long (usually from calling external I/O inside a tx)
- watch `hikaricp_connections_pending` — a rising pending count means the pool is exhausted

Deep dive: with virtual threads, don't oversize the pool thinking it 'scales' — DB connections are still finite, so protect them with a pool + semaphore.
:::

items.q: Testing strategy for a Spring Boot service: test pyramid, slice tests, Testcontainers, contract tests?
items.a:
Follow the [[g:test pyramid]]:
- lots of [[b:unit tests]] (JUnit 5 + Mockito, pure domain logic, milliseconds)
- fewer: [[b:integration tests]]
- on top: a handful of [[b:e2e tests]]

- Spring [[g:slice tests]] (`@WebMvcTest`, `@DataJpaTest`) load only part of the context → fast
- test real infrastructure (DB, Kafka) with [[g:Testcontainers]] (Docker) instead of H2, to stay close to production
- [[g:contract tests]] (Spring Cloud Contract/Pact) keep provider–consumer compatibility from breaking when APIs change

:::deep
[[r:Anti-pattern]]: cramming every test into `@SpringBootTest` (loads the whole context → slow, brittle) instead of using slice/unit tests.

**[[r:H2 lies]]**: its dialect/locking/data types differ from MySQL/Postgres → tests pass green but production fails; Testcontainers runs the real engine inside Docker.

- [[r:Flaky tests]] are usually caused by time/order/thread dependencies → replace `Thread.sleep` with Awaitility, isolate data per test
- fintech/OTA: test *idempotency* (calling twice with the same key → one effect) + *concurrency* (two threads debiting money/booking a seat at once → correct final balance)
- *property-based testing* (jqwik) for money calculations (BigDecimal, rounding); measure quality with *mutation testing* (PIT), not just coverage %
:::

items.q: The full bean lifecycle: what are the 8 stages, and where do the intervention hooks sit?
items.a:
The container doesn't just `new` an object — it runs [[b:8 stages]] for every bean. Knowing the exact order is how you answer 'when does the AOP proxy get created' and 'why has `@PostConstruct` already seen its dependencies'. 1. [[b:Instantiation]] — calls the constructor (constructor injection happens right here) 2. [[b:Populate properties]] — sets fields/setters: `@Autowired`, `@Value` 3. [[b:Aware callbacks]] — `BeanNameAware` → `BeanFactoryAware` → `ApplicationContextAware` 4. [[b:BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization]] — runs for *every* bean 5. [[b:Initialization]] — `@PostConstruct` → `afterPropertiesSet()` (InitializingBean) → `init-method` 6. [[b:BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization]] — [[g:where the AOP proxy gets wrapped]] 7. [[b:Ready to use]] — the singleton sits in the container, serving requests 8. [[b:Destruction]] — `@PreDestroy` → `destroy()` (DisposableBean) → `destroy-method` :::warn Trap [[r:Prototype]] beans: the container creates them and lets go — it [[r:never calls the destroy callback]]. Resources (files, sockets, executors) in a prototype bean must be closed manually. ::: :::deep - `@PostConstruct` runs in step 5, [[o:before the proxy is wrapped in step 6]] → `this` at that point is the [[r:raw bean]]; calling your own `@Transactional`/`@Async`/`@Cacheable` method from within `@PostConstruct` has no effect - if you need to run after the context is fully ready, use `ApplicationRunner`/`CommandLineRunner` or `@EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent.class)` - `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` modifies the [[b:BeanDefinition]] (metadata — before instantiation); `BeanPostProcessor` modifies the [[b:instance]] (after instantiation). Confusing the two is a classic mistake - BPPs are initialized very early → [[r:don't inject business beans into a BeanPostProcessor]]: that bean gets created before the infrastructure is ready and [[r:permanently loses its chance to be post-processed]] (no proxy → loses `@Transactional`) - `@PreDestroy` only runs on a graceful context shutdown (SIGTERM + shutdown hook); `kill -9`/an OOM-kill skips it → [[o:don't put critical business logic in a destroy callback]] - destruction order is the reverse of initialization order; to control start/stop order use `@DependsOn` or `SmartLifecycle` (with `getPhase()`) **Where each hook sits among the 8 stages:** 
@Component
class GdsClient implements InitializingBean, DisposableBean {
    
    GdsClient(HttpPool pool) { /* ... */ }         // 1 · constructor injection
    
    @Autowired void setClock(Clock c) { }        // 2 · populate field/setter
    
    @PostConstruct void warmUp() {              // 5 · after *Aware and BPP.before
        this.refreshCache();                     // @Cacheable here has NO EFFECT: proxy not wrapped yet
    }
    
    public void afterPropertiesSet() { }          // 5 · right after @PostConstruct
    
    public void destroy() { }                     // 8 · only runs on a graceful context shutdown
}
    
// The proxy (@Transactional, @Async, @Cacheable) is wrapped in stage 6 — AFTER stage 5.
// If you need to run once everything is truly ready: @EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent.class).
:::

items.q: How does a request flow through DispatcherServlet? Filter vs Interceptor vs ArgumentResolver vs MessageConverter?
items.a: `DispatcherServlet` is the [[g:front controller]]: it doesn't handle business logic, only dispatches. - [[b:1 HandlerMapping]] — finds the handler matching `@RequestMapping` (path, method, header, produces/consumes) - [[b:2 HandlerExecutionChain]] — runs `Interceptor.preHandle()` in registration order - [[b:3 HandlerAdapter]] — `InvocableHandlerMethod` invokes the controller method - [[b:3.1 ArgumentResolver]] — deserializes JSON → DTO, `@Valid`, `@RequestParam`, `@PathVariable` - [[b:3.2 → 3.4]] — Controller (`@RestController`) → Service (`@Transactional`) → Repository - [[b:3.5 ReturnValueHandler]] + [[b:3.6 HttpMessageConverter]] — Jackson serializes the object → JSON - [[b:4 postHandle]] — only runs when there is *no* exception - [[b:5 HandlerExceptionResolver]] — maps exceptions → HTTP status (`@ControllerAdvice`) - [[b:6 afterCompletion]] — always runs, even on error → cleans up MDC/ThreadLocal **Filter vs Interceptor:** a Filter belongs to the [[o:Servlet spec]], wrapping *outside* DispatcherServlet — it sees the raw request/response and can short-circuit (Security returns 401, rate limiting returns 429). An Interceptor belongs to [[o:Spring MVC]], sitting *inside* DispatcherServlet, so it knows which `HandlerMethod` is about to run. :::warn Trap An exception thrown [[r:inside a filter]] (e.g. a broken token in the Security filter) [[r:does not go through `@ControllerAdvice`]] — it has already left DispatcherServlet. For a consistent JSON error body you must configure `AuthenticationEntryPoint`/`ErrorController`. ::: :::deep - `@Transactional` commits at step 3.3, but Jackson serializes at [[b:3.6 — after the tx has already closed]] → touching a lazy collection at that point throws `LazyInitializationException`. Fix with a fetch join/DTO projection, [[r:not with `spring.jpa.open-in-view`]] (defaults to true: keeps the EntityManager open for the whole request → holds the connection longer and masks N+1 queries) - a filter that sets MDC/correlation id [[r:must call `MDC.clear()` in a `finally`]] — worker threads are reused, so without clearing, this request's log lines carry the previous request's traceId - filter order: `@Order`/`FilterRegistrationBean.setOrder`; Spring Security is actually *one* filter (`FilterChainProxy`) containing an internal chain of sub-filters - `produces`/`consumes` participate in handler selection and determine which `HttpMessageConverter` is used; duplicate mappings for the same path fail immediately at startup (`AmbiguousMappingException`) - `ArgumentResolver`/`ReturnValueHandler` are customized via `WebMvcConfigurer` — the standard place to implement `@CurrentUser` or a standardized response envelope :::
